description: Append-only Analyst run history. Every run appends one record; nothing is ever overwritten or edited. Each record carries the timestamp, the model and effort level it ran at, both passes verbatim, the verdict, the confidence, the pre-registered falsifier, the input-snapshot hash, token counts and computed cost. The input hash is the load-bearing field: without it you cannot audit why a past verdict looked reasonable at the time. The app does not read this file - it reads dissent_log.json - so records here can be as detailed as the audit needs.

**What the call rests on, stated plainly, and it is weak.** No alarm threshold on this dashboard is tripped. One attention line is crossed (worker share of income, 1.18 SD). The verdict is AUGMENTATION at low confidence: productivity is accelerating into the internet-boom band while the exposed-vs-control jobs gap is flat-to-narrowing, exposed job postings have improved slightly over six months, and total payrolls are still positive. That is productivity gains without an accelerating displacement signature. It is not a clean augmentation picture — exposed employment is outright contracting and labor's income share just set a 79-year low — and I say below exactly how each supporting panel reads the other way.

---

**Panel: labor_productivity (2.8%, 2026-03, up from 2.5%)**

In the 2.7–3.4 band for one quarter. The break rule needs >3.4 for two straight quarters; we are not close. Baseline has 31 readings against 36 needed, so I will not attach a sigma to this and will not call 2.8 "unusual" — I read it as direction only: rising, and at a pace that is fast by post-2010 standards.

I cite it as supporting augmentation because rising output per hour alongside still-positive aggregate payrolls (+57k, unemployment 4.2%) is the arithmetic of more output per worker rather than fewer workers.

*Inversion — the strongest displacement reading of this same number:* output per hour is a ratio, and this panel gives me neither the numerator nor the denominator. Productivity accelerating from 2.5 to 2.8 in the same window where exposed-industry employment is running -1.3% YoY and labor's share of income fell four consecutive quarters is precisely the displacement arithmetic: hours in the denominator get cut, output holds, the ratio rises, and the gains show up in capital's share rather than labor's. On this dashboard I genuinely cannot separate those two stories from the productivity panel alone — the labor-share panel is the only cross-check, and it points the displacement way. This is the single weakest link in my call and I want it on the record.

**Panel: exposed_vs_control_jobs (exposed -1.3%, control +1.3%, differential -2.5, 2026-06)**

Differential is 0.26 SD toward displacement against a calm-period mean of -2.19 — essentially at its own normal. Prior month -2.61, so the gap narrowed 0.11pp. Twenty-one consecutive readings inside normal range. Alarm trigger is -4.8; we are 2.3 points away. The panel's own rule is explicit: a wide steady gap is not the alarm, the widening is. There is no widening.

*Inversion — the strongest displacement reading:* the differential is normal, but the level is not benign. Exposed employment is shrinking in absolute terms (-1.3% YoY across information, professional/business services and financial activities) while control grows at +1.3%. A gap that is "steady" at a contracting level is a steady drain, and twenty-one months of it compounds to real headcount. Worse, the baseline that makes -2.5 look normal starts in 2017-07 and spans the entire period in which knowledge-work hiring was already deteriorating — so "normal" here may already encode the phenomenon I am supposed to be detecting, and a mean-reverting differential proves only that the drain is not accelerating, not that it is absent. Also note control's +1.3% is itself soft; a narrowing gap driven by control weakening rather than exposed recovering would be a false comfort. The payload does not let me decompose that, and it should. I take this inversion seriously; it is why the falsifier sits on this panel.

**Panel: job_postings_spread (-28, 2026-07; +3 over six months)**

Spread 0.21 SD toward displacement, 19 months inside normal, trigger at -67. Postings lead hiring, so a spread that is drifting *less* negative is the leading indicator refusing to confirm a coming jobs alarm. That is the second leg of my call.

*Inversion:* the improvement is 3 index points on a series with a standard deviation of 22 — statistically indistinguishable from flat, and I should not lean on it as a trend. Meanwhile the level says exposed knowledge-work postings sit at 76 versus Feb-2020=100 while control sits at 104. Exposed demand is a quarter below pre-pandemic while hands-on demand is above it. A displacement reading of that is: the adjustment already happened, postings found a permanently lower plateau, and the "normal range" I am comforting myself with is normal only because the baseline starts in 2022 and thus contains the entire collapse from the 2022 boom (high +37.2 in 2022-02, low -42.7 in 2023-10). A wide calm SD built from a crash makes a depressed steady state look unremarkable. This series also has no pre-pandemic anchor, per its own caveat, so I hold it more loosely than the CES panels.

**Panel: exposed_vs_control_wages (exposed 4.6, control 3.5, differential +1.1, 2026-06; prior +0.71)**

Face value this is the prettiest augmentation number on the board: pay in AI-exposed industries pulling 1.1pp ahead of control, 0.76 SD *away* from displacement, and widening month over month. I am not citing it as strong support, because the panel's weighting rule forbids it: exposed employment is falling (-1.27% YoY), so the composition mechanism is live — the average can rise because lower-paid exposed workers exited, with nobody getting a raise. The control side is contaminated in the mirror direction, since growing low-wage leisure/hospitality drags the control average down. So this panel cannot distinguish the two verdicts here and I treat it as uninformative rather than as evidence.

*Inversion (which is really the artifact itself):* under displacement, +1.1 is exactly what you expect — thinning-from-the-bottom in the exposed group plus low-wage growth in the control group produces a widening pay differential with zero raises anywhere. That reading is fully available and I cannot rule it out. What I *can* say is that the panel is nowhere near its own displacement trigger (-2.4); exposed pay collapsing relative to control, which is the signature of exposed workers competing against cheap capability, is not happening.

**Panel: worker_share_of_income (51.0%, 2026-03; -1.0 over 4 quarters; 4 consecutive declines)**

This is the strongest displacement evidence in the payload and it argues against my verdict. The level is the lowest in 309 readings back to 1947. The 4-quarter change is 1.18 SD toward displacement, past the attention line, with the alarm trigger at -1.5 versus -1.0 actual. Four straight quarterly declines is a trend, not a print.

Why it does not flip the call: the panel's own rule says acceleration, not level, is the tell — and the record-low *level* is the tail of a decades-long secular slide that long predates any AI deployment, so I refuse to score the 1947-baseline record as an AI event. On acceleration we are between attention and alarm, and -1.0 against a historical low of -2.18 (2009-12) is a moderate, not extreme, four-quarter move. Combined with rising productivity, though, this is the one place where the displacement story has both a mechanism and a moving number, and if it reaches -1.5 my call is in trouble even without the jobs gap moving. Listed as secondary falsifier below.

**Panel: recent_grad_gap (2.6pp, above trailing 10-year average, 100 consecutive months)**

Supplemental by rule; does not move the headline. Displacement-leaning in tone, but 100 consecutive months reaches back to roughly 2018 — this gap has been positive continuously since well before capable generative models existed, which makes it a chronic feature of the entry-level market rather than a deployment signal. Being above its own trailing 10-year average is worth watching, since the entry level is where handoff-capable automation would bite first; it is not evidence I can weight here.

**Panel: ai_adoption (21.7% of firms, 2026-07; 17.3% in 2025-11)**

Direction over nine collections is unambiguously up, roughly +4.4pp, and the one flat month (20.6 → 20.6) is noise by the artifact's own instruction. So the weak-form deployment gate is open: real adoption exists, a displacement reading is permitted. It causes nothing on its own, and I do not treat rising adoption as evidence for either verdict — it is the precondition.

One gap I want flagged: the artifact says "the size-class series below is the check" and directs me to test whether adoption is concentrated in the largest firms, because one-firm-one-vote at 21.7% means something very different if the adopters employ millions. That size-class series is not in the payload. I therefore cannot convert the firm share into headcount exposure, and that is a real hole in the case for *either* side. If adoption turns out to be concentrated in large employers, my augmentation call is standing on thinner ice than the panels suggest.

**Panel: ai_use_automation_vs_augmentation (43.1 automation / 56.9 augmentation, 2025-09-15)**

Three releases, essentially flat (42.6/57.4 → 43.1/56.9 → 43.1/56.9). Read as weak directional context only, per its rule: the majority of sampled use is augmentative and that has not moved. Latest reading is 2025-09, ten months stale relative to the labor panels, over a rotating user base, one vendor, conversations not jobs.

*Inversion:* 43.1% automation is not a small number, and a *constant* share against rising adoption means the absolute volume of automated tasks is climbing. A stable ratio is not reassurance; it is a ratio holding while the denominator grows. And the mix could be stable for the mechanical reason the artifact names — who shows up to use the product changed — while individual work practice shifted underneath. I give this panel very little weight in either direction and would not have cited it if the rule allowed more.

**Panel: macro_regime (real 10y 2.4, 10y-2y +0.4, 10y-3m not inverted, expected inflation 2.2)**

Curve is positive, so the bond market is not independently pricing an ordinary recession. Two consequences, and they cut in opposite directions. First, it removes the cleanest confounder available: I cannot attribute exposed-sector weakness to a cycle the bond market is already forecasting, which is why I did not go CONFOUNDED. Second — and this cuts against me — if softness in exposed industries is not cyclical, that makes the structural (AI) reading of exposed contraction *more* rather than less available. I note this honestly: the macro panel is not a point in favor of augmentation, it is a point against the recession excuse, and it slightly strengthens the case I am ruling against.

**Capability panels (METR, GDPval-AA Elo, GDPval vs experts, benchmark tracks)**

Descriptive only; they vote on nothing and I did not let them. For the record: METR's 80% horizon leader at 186 minutes on clean, self-contained, auto-scorable software/ML/cyber tasks with no-context contractor baselines — not the messy parts of a job, and the rule explicitly says this stopped conditioning anything in July 2026. The Elo pool has no human in it, so levels are meaningless and only the 113.8-point gap carries information; ratings are frozen to pool v2 and I made no cross-version comparison. GDPval wins-plus-ties at 70.9% is *not* parity — true parity is 50% wins-only and the model sits at 49.7%, self-reported by the lab that owns the benchmark, and nothing has been published since 2025-12. I extended no trend into that gap. HLE 53, SWE-bench 87, LAB-Bench 75, none saturated. Capability is clearly advancing; none of it is a labor observation, and letting a software benchmark decide a labor verdict is the error the rules are written to prevent.

---

**Hypotheses I generated and rejected**

*Ordinary cyclical slowdown as the driver of exposed weakness.* Rejected as a confounder: the yield curve is positive (+0.4 on 10y-2y, 10y-3m not inverted), unemployment is 4.2%, payrolls positive. There is no independent recession pricing to point at. Also, the exposed-minus-control construction is designed to net out aggregate cooling, and that differential is flat at 0.26 SD.

*Sector-specific unwind of the 2021-22 tech/professional hiring bubble.* This is the most credible non-AI story for exposed contraction and postings at 76, and the postings baseline high of +37.2 in 2022-02 falling to -42.7 by 2023-10 is consistent with it. I rejected it as a stated confounder for two reasons: it would predict continued *improvement* off the trough, which is roughly what the +3 six-month spread change shows and which supports my directional call anyway; and the payload has no series that separates bubble-unwind from AI substitution, so naming it would be asserting a mechanism I cannot evidence. CONFOUNDED requires a named cause *plus* the series that supports it, and I do not have the second half.

*Composition-driven wage differential as evidence of augmentation.* Rejected outright by the weighting rule. Exposed employment is falling, so I set the panel aside rather than bank it.

*Record-low labor share as an AI event.* Rejected on level, retained on acceleration. A 1947-anchored record in a series with a decades-long downtrend is not attributable to a technology deployed in the last three years; the four-quarter change at 1.18 SD is the part that is live, and it is below alarm.

**News package — considered, and what I did with each**

*BLS Employment Situation through 2026-06: payrolls 158,984k, +57k, unemployment 4.2%.* This is ground truth and it does bear on the call. +57k is a soft month by historical standards but positive, and 4.2% unemployment is not a labor market in distress. It corroborates the "exposed sectors shrinking inside a still-growing whole" picture rather than a broad contraction, which is the pattern augmentation-with-reallocation looks like. Revisions are legitimate veto material; none were supplied, so nothing to veto with. If a future package carries large downward revisions to spring payrolls, the aggregate cushion under this call gets thinner.

*AP: "inflation economy iran trump unemployment."* An Iran conflict is a plausible macro shock — energy prices, freight, general hiring caution — and it generates a hypothesis worth naming. I set it aside as a driver of these readings for three reasons. It is too recent to be inside a 2026-06 CES reading or a 2026-03 productivity and labor-share print. Its transmission channel is energy-intensive and goods-facing, which would hit the *control* group (construction, leisure/hospitality) hardest — yet control is the side that is *growing* at +1.3%. And it offers no mechanism at all for why pay growth in information/professional/financial runs 1.1pp ahead of control, or why labor's income share had already declined for four straight quarters ending in March. Expected inflation at 2.2% and a real 10-year yield of 2.4% show no bond-market stress consistent with a live energy shock either.

*AP: "job openings economy trump iran war hiring."* Points at a hiring slowdown, which is consistent with +57k payrolls and with control growth at only 1.3%. It is directionally relevant context but it is aggregate, not exposure-specific, and the dashboard's exposed-minus-control design already differences out an economy-wide hiring chill. A generalized slowdown cannot explain a *differential*, and the differential is where the AI signal has to live. Set aside for the verdict; noted as a reason not to read control's +1.3% as strength.

Neither wire item changed the verdict, and by rule neither could have strengthened it. Both were checked for a specific mechanism that would move a specific panel; neither survived that check.

**Cross-panel observations**

The tension worth naming: productivity up, exposed employment down, labor share down. Two of those three are the displacement signature. What holds the augmentation call together is that the *differences* — jobs gap, postings spread, wage gap — are all sitting at or better than their own calm-period norms, and every alarm trigger is distant (jobs -4.8 vs -2.5; postings -67 vs -28; wages -2.4 vs +1.1; labor-share change -1.5 vs -1.0). This dashboard is built so that the widening, not the width, is the alarm. Nothing is widening this month. That is the whole case, and it is a case about second derivatives, which is a thin thing to stand on.

The most dangerous combination to watch is labor share and productivity moving together: if output per hour clears 3.4 for two quarters while the four-quarter labor-share change reaches -1.5, the productivity gains are demonstrably not flowing to workers and my inversion of the productivity panel becomes the correct reading of it. That configuration would flip this call even with the jobs gap still flat.

**Falsifier, machine-checkable (primary):** exposed_vs_control_jobs — differential_exposed_minus_control falls to -3.5 percentage points or lower in any monthly reading published on or before 2026-10-26. (That is one full SD past the -2.19 calm-period mean, and it would end the 21-month in-range streak.)

**Secondary tripwires, same 2026-10-26 horizon, any one of which materially damages this call even if the primary holds:** (a) worker_share_of_income four-quarter change reaches -1.5 percentage points or worse, hitting its own alarm trigger; (b) labor_productivity prints above 3.4 percent for a second consecutive quarter; (c) job_postings_spread widens to -40 or beyond, reversing the six-month improvement I leaned on.

**Falsifier, plain:** The exposed-vs-control jobs chart moves first — if that gap drops to -3.5 or worse, the gap is widening rather than holding, and I was wrong.

*AP: "inflation economy iran trump unemployment."* An Iran conflict is a plausible macro shock — energy prices, freight, general hiring caution — and it generates a hypothesis worth naming. I set it aside as a driver of these readings for three reasons. It is too recent to be inside a 2026-06 CES reading or a 2026-03 productivity and labor-share print. Its transmission channel is energy-intensive and goods-facing, which would hit the *control* group (construction, leisure/hospitality) hardest — yet control is the side that is *growing* at +1.3%. And it offers no mechanism at all for why pay growth in information/professional/financial runs 1.1pp ahead of control, or why labor's income share had already declined for four straight quarters ending in March. Expected inflation at 2.2% and a real 10-year yield of 2.4% show no bond-market stress consistent with a live energy shock either.

*AP: "job openings economy trump iran war hiring."* Points at a hiring slowdown, which is consistent with +57k payrolls and with control growth at only 1.3%. It is directionally relevant context but it is aggregate, not exposure-specific, and the dashboard's exposed-minus-control design already differences out an economy-wide hiring chill. A generalized slowdown cannot explain a *differential*, and the differential is where the AI signal has to live. Set aside for the verdict; noted as a reason not to read control's +1.3% as strength.

Neither wire item changed the verdict, and by rule neither could have strengthened it. Both were checked for a specific mechanism that would move a specific panel; neither survived that check.

**Cross-panel observations**

The tension worth naming: productivity up, exposed employment down, labor share down. Two of those three are the displacement signature. What holds the augmentation call together is that the *differences* — jobs gap, postings spread, wage gap — are all sitting at or better than their own calm-period norms, and every alarm trigger is distant (jobs -4.8 vs -2.5; postings -67 vs -28; wages -2.4 vs +1.1; labor-share change -1.5 vs -1.0). This dashboard is built so that the widening, not the width, is the alarm. Nothing is widening this month. That is the whole case, and it is a case about second derivatives, which is a thin thing to stand on.

The most dangerous combination to watch is labor share and productivity moving together: if output per hour clears 3.4 for two quarters while the four-quarter labor-share change reaches -1.5, the productivity gains are demonstrably not flowing to workers and my inversion of the productivity panel becomes the correct reading of it. That configuration would flip this call even with the jobs gap still flat.

**Falsifier, machine-checkable (primary):** exposed_vs_control_jobs — differential_exposed_minus_control falls to -3.5 percentage points or lower in any monthly reading published on or before 2026-10-26. (That is one full SD past the -2.19 calm-period mean, and it would end the 21-month in-range streak.)

**Secondary tripwires, same 2026-10-26 horizon, any one of which materially damages this call even if the primary holds:** (a) worker_share_of_income four-quarter change reaches -1.5 percentage points or worse, hitting its own alarm trigger; (b) labor_productivity prints above 3.4 percent for a second consecutive quarter; (c) job_postings_spread widens to -40 or beyond, reversing the six-month improvement I leaned on.

**Falsifier, plain:** The exposed-vs-control jobs chart moves first — if that gap drops to -3.5 or worse, the gap is widening rather than holding, and I was wrong.

pass2.publishedNote:
AI still looks like it is helping workers more than replacing them, but this is the thinnest version of that call yet.

This is the first note in this format, so there is no prior edition to measure against. In the data itself, no alarm line was crossed this month. One early-warning line was: the share of national income that goes to workers rather than to owners of capital has now fallen four quarters running and sits at its lowest point in records that begin in 1947.

The strongest support for the call is the shape of the exposed job market. Employment in information, professional and business services, and finance is shrinking, running about 1.3% below a year ago, while industries AI has barely touched are growing by roughly the same amount in the opposite direction. That gap is wide, but it has been about this wide for a long stretch, and in the latest reading it narrowed slightly rather than opening further. Job postings in exposed fields have drifted marginally less negative in recent months. At the same time, output per hour worked is accelerating, near 2.8%, with total payrolls still adding jobs and unemployment steady. More output alongside a still-growing workforce is the arithmetic of people doing more, not of people being removed. What triggers concern here is a gap that is widening, not one that is merely wide, and nothing is widening.

The strongest argument the other way is that output per hour is a ratio, and it rises either when output grows or when the hours underneath it are cut. Shrinking employment in exposed industries, combined with four consecutive quarterly declines in labor's income share, is precisely what the second version looks like: the gains from the technology showing up with capital rather than in paychecks. From these figures alone, the two stories cannot be told apart.

There is a similar trap in pay. Wages in AI-heavy industries are growing faster than elsewhere, 4.6% against 3.5%, which reads as reassuring until you notice that an industry losing jobs can see its average wage rise simply because lower-paid workers left. Nobody need have received a raise. That figure is therefore set aside rather than counted as evidence. And the weakness in exposed industries has no convenient excuse available: the bond market is not pricing a recession, which removes the ordinary business cycle as the explanation and makes the structural reading more plausible, not less.

What to watch: the exposed-versus-control jobs chart. If that gap drops clearly below the range it has held for the past couple of years, the wide-but-steady reading dies and this call flips.
